analysis.one_liner: Restricts how employers collect and use worker data, requires disclosure of workplace surveillance, and creates a Labor Department enforcement office.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 23, 2026, the bill has 9 Democratic cosponsors and has gone no further than referral to three House committees.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar employers with 11 or more workers from using workplace data to identify who is organizing a union, who has reported the employer to authorities, or workers' off-duty political and religious lives. It would require employers to tell workers in plain language exactly what data is collected on them, how, and how it feeds hiring, firing, and promotion decisions, and would let workers see and correct that data. It would create a new Worker Protection and Technology Division inside the Labor Department to enforce the rules, give workers a right to sue with statutory damages, and void arbitration clauses for these claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants at employers with 11 or more employees, including app-based and contract workers, who are increasingly tracked through software that logs keystrokes, location, messages, biometrics, and productivity scores. The bill would stop employers from using that data to detect union organizing or whistleblowing, ban collection in bathrooms, lactation rooms, and workers' homes off-shift, ban selling worker data, and give workers a way to see, correct, and contest the data used against them in work decisions.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits collecting or using employee data to identify workers who are or want to be union members, monitor protected organizing activity, or identify workers who report the employer for breaking the law [S2].
Bars off-duty data collection in break rooms, restrooms, locker rooms, lactation rooms, prayer spaces, and workers' homes or remote work locations [S2].
Bans selling or licensing worker data and blocks most transfers to third parties; transfers to service providers require disclosure and worker opt-in [S2].

Requires employers to disclose in plain language what data is collected, how, where it is stored, who has access, and how it affects hiring, firing, discipline, scheduling, and promotion decisions, and lets workers obtain and correct their data within 30 days and ask for reconsideration of a data-driven decision [S2].

Creates a Worker Protection and Technology Division in the Labor Department with an appointed Administrator, advisory boards including labor representatives, and Wage and Hour Division enforcement powers, plus whistleblower anti-retaliation protections with statutory damages up to $50,000 per violation [S2].

Gives workers and unions a private right to sue with damages of at least twice actual damages and $5,000-$40,000 statutory damages for data violations, and voids predispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for these claims [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 11 or more workers, including private companies, public agencies, and Congressional and executive-branch offices, would bear the cost of auditing their data collection, rewriting disclosures and service-provider contracts, deleting data on schedule, and defending lawsuits. Workplace-surveillance and people-analytics vendors would lose sales as employers shrink or drop monitoring programs to comply.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers and surveillance software vendors

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are real: employers would need to inventory every data stream, produce plain-language disclosures in each worker's primary language, rewrite vendor contracts, and delete data three years after separation, costs that small employers near the 11-worker threshold and public agencies would feel too [S2].

The 'least invasive means' and 'strictly necessary' standards for any data collection are demanding, and employers would face statutory damages of $5,000-$40,000 per violation plus private suits and union lawsuits, which critics would call a litigation burden that could deter legitimate productivity, safety, and security monitoring [S2].

Restricting collection of health status, predictive behavioral data, and device usage may limit some employer programs for safety, fraud prevention, and quality control that the bill itself acknowledges as legitimate purposes, forcing a case-by-case judgment that regulators would have to work out in rulemaking [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to workers are substantial and specific: an end to secret union-activity and whistleblower surveillance, off-duty snooping, and undisclosed algorithmic scoring, backed by real enforcement money and a right to sue without arbitration. The costs are real but conventional regulatory compliance costs; the bill's biggest design risk is its broad private right of action and per-violation damages, which courts and rulemakers would have to keep from becoming a fishing expedition. On balance the consumer protections outweigh the compliance burden, though the litigation exposure is the strongest honest objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to three House committees — Education and Workforce, Oversight and Government Reform, and House Administration — and none has taken it up, so it sits waiting for a markup that has not been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Deluzio, joined by Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, introduced the bill on June 23, 2026 [S1] [S2].

The Speaker referred it to the Committee on Education and Workforce and, in addition, to Oversight and Government Reform and House Administration, a multi-committee referral that divides jurisdiction and makes passage harder [S4].
Nine House Democrats had cosponsored the bill, with no Republican cosponsors, as of the latest record [S3].
No committee has reported the bill, and no floor action, hearing, or vote appears in the action history [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers and workplace-surveillance software vendors, since the restrictions they would face have not advanced an inch. Workers gain nothing unless the bill moves.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and surveillance vendors, so far

for.name: Rep. Chris Deluzio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction as an original cosponsor.

against.name: House Republican committee chairs (Education and Workforce, Oversight, House Administration)
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Have not scheduled any markup, hearing, or floor consideration of the bill; it sits unreferred-to-action in all three committees.

sides.party_line_note: All ten supporters are Democrats in a House where Republicans hold 223 of 440 seats, and no Republican has cosponsored; the lack of any committee action follows the majority party's position.

industries.industry: Workplace surveillance and people-analytics software vendors
industries.note: These firms sell keystroke, location, biometric, and productivity-monitoring systems to employers; the bill bans many of those uses, bans selling worker data, and requires disclosure of what is collected, shrinking their market. Their business model profits from exactly the collection workers cannot currently see or contest.

industries.industry: Large employers (11 or more workers), including app-based staffing platforms
industries.note: Employers would lose the ability to quietly track union activity, whistleblowing, off-duty behavior, and health status, and would take on compliance and litigation exposure; in exchange they keep lawful uses for safety, quality, and bona fide performance reviews. Their interest in cheap, invisible monitoring runs against workers' interest in knowing and limiting it.

industries.industry: Biometric and AI hiring-screening tool makers
industries.note: The bill treats fingerprints, face and gait templates as protected employee data, requires disclosure of automated decision systems, and lets workers see and contest the inputs to algorithmic hiring and firing decisions, directly constraining these products.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, a tri-committee referral, and only nine cosponsors total three months into the session's final stretch, the bill is unlikely to get a markup or floor vote; the realistic path is dying in committee at the end of the 119th Congress, unless worker-surveillance provisions are attached to a larger package.
